title: Block close: room for your question
hookLine: midrash teaches that the text has room for your question too
tomorrow: did the conversation stop when the Talmud was finished?

cards: A secondhand book, and someone else's pencil in the margins: an underline, a question mark, a small "really?" next to a line. Holding a book like that, you're holding a conversation between two strangers and a page.
That is what midrash looks like from the inside. So after forty days of it, yesterday's question: is there any room left for yours?

teach.h: EVERY ANSWER STARTED AS A QUESTION.
teach.b: Look back at this block and every answer started as a question. Why does the wanting double? Why is Rachel heard when Moses isn't?
Who stood afar off at the river? What is a Hebrew name doing on Pharaoh's daughter? The text didn't say.
Someone asked, and the answer became midrash.

teach.h: TURN IT, AND TURN IT AGAIN.
teach.b: In Pirkei Avot, Ben Bag Bag says of the Torah: turn it, and turn it again, for everything is in it.
A midrash on Numbers says the Torah has seventy faces. Not one face copied seventy times: seventy ways of looking.
And the tradition kept the arguments, not only the winners. That's why you heard Rabbi Meir beside Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Joshua beside Rabban Yochanan.
One to tell a friend tonight: the Mishnah explains why it records opinions that lost, so a later court can lean on them someday.
So yes, there's room. Midrash doesn't close the text. It shows how to open it: read closely, notice what's odd, ask honestly, stay inside the words.
Your question joins everyone who ever leaned over the same page.

how: Jewish study is often done in pairs (chavruta), reading a text aloud and questioning it together; printed pages of the Talmud set the commentaries around the text in the margins.

o: a rule that only rabbis may add to a text

games.q: in class, a friend asks a question about a story everyone thinks is obvious, and a few people laugh. by the way midrash reads, what's true?
o: noticing something odd in a text is exactly how midrash begins.
only experts' questions belong in a conversation like that.
a good text has one meaning, so the question was off track.
games.why: every answer in this block began as someone noticing what the text didn't say. turn it, and turn it again.

practice: Pick up a pen and any paper, and choose one line you know, from this block, a psalm, or a prayer. Write it by hand in the middle of the page and leave wide margins.
In the margin, write one question you'd ask it, and if one comes, a single line of answer. Feel the pen move; that's a midrash in miniature, and the whole sit is yours for it.

wordCard.voice: Block close: forty days of reading midrash, from the arithmetic of wanting to the four children, and a margin left open for you.

orig.note: Hebrew: seventy faces to the Torah, a midrash's picture of many ways of reading.

carryVoice: There's room for your question, in the margin, right beside theirs. Forty of forty: the block is done.
